topic: Degree of Dissociation from van 't Hoff Factor
questionText: A $0.1\text{ M}$ aqueous solution of an electrolyte $AB_2$ exhibits a van 't Hoff factor of $i = 2.60$. What is the percentage degree of dissociation ($\alpha$) of this electrolyte?

options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle
Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle
Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle
Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution:
For $AB_2 \to A^{2+} + 2B^-$, the number of ions per formula unit is $n = 3$.
The formula relating degree of dissociation to $i$ is:
$\alpha = \frac{i - 1}{n - 1} = \frac{2.60 - 1}{3 - 1} = \frac{1.60}{2} = 0.80 = 80\%$.

questionText: Which of the following $0.10\text{ M}$ aqueous solutions will exhibit the HIGHEST boiling point at $1\text{ atm}$ atmospheric pressure?

options.text: $0.10\text{ M } FeCl_3$
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.text: $0.10\text{ M } BaCl_2$
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: $0.10\text{ M } NaCl$
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: $0.10\text{ M } Glucose$
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution:
Elevation in boiling point is $\Delta T_b = i K_b m$. Assuming complete dissociation:
Glucose: $i = 1 \implies i \cdot m = 0.10$
$NaCl$: $i = 2 \implies i \cdot m = 0.20$
$BaCl_2$: $i = 3 \implies i \cdot m = 0.30$
$FeCl_3$: $i = 4 \implies i \cdot m = 0.40$
$FeCl_3$ produces the greatest effective particle concentration and therefore the highest boiling point.

questionText: Which of the following $0.05\text{ M}$ aqueous solutions will exhibit the LOWEST freezing point?

options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle
Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: $0.05\text{ M } KCl$
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: $0.05\text{ M } Urea$
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution:
Freezing point depression is $\Delta T_f = i K_f m$, and Freezing Point = $0^\circ\text{C} - \Delta T_f$. The lowest freezing point corresponds to the greatest depression $\Delta T_f$ (largest $i \cdot m$ product).
$Al_2(SO_4)_3$ has $i = 5$, giving $i \cdot m = 5 \times 0.05 = 0.25$, which is higher than $K_2SO_4$ ($i=3, 0.15$), $KCl$ ($i=2, 0.10$), and urea ($i=1, 0.05$).

questionText: A $5\%$ (m/V) solution of cane sugar (sucrose, molar mass $= 342\text{ g/mol}$) is isotonic with a $0.877\%$ (m/V) solution of an unknown organic substance X. What is the molar mass of X?

options.text: $60\text{ g/mol}$
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.text: $180\text{ g/mol}$
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: $120\text{ g/mol}$
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: $90\text{ g/mol}$
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution:
Isotonic solutions have equal molar concentrations: $C_1 = C_2$.
$\frac{w_1}{M_1 V_1} = \frac{w_2}{M_2 V_2} \implies \frac{5\text{ g}}{342} = \frac{0.877\text{ g}}{M_2} \implies M_2 = \frac{0.877 \times 342}{5} = \frac{299.9}{5} \approx 60\text{ g/mol}$ (corresponding to urea).

questionText: If the half-life ($t_{1/2}$) of a reaction is found to be inversely proportional to the initial concentration of the reactant ($t_{1/2} \propto \frac{1}{[A]_0}$), what is the order of the reaction?

options.text: Second order
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.text: First order
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: Zero order
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: Third order
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution:
The general relationship is $t_{1/2} \propto [A]_0^{1-n}$.
For $t_{1/2} \propto [A]_0^{-1}$, we have $1 - n = -1 \implies n = 2$ (second order).

questionText: A zero-order reaction has a rate constant $k = 0.002\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ s}^{-1}$. If the initial concentration of the reactant is $0.20\text{ M}$, what is its half-life?

options.text: $50\text{ s}$
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle
Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: $25\text{ s}$
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle
Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution: For zero-order: $t_{1/2} = \frac{[A]_0}{2k} = \frac{0.20\text{ mol/L}}{2 \times 0.002\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ s}^{-1}} = \frac{0.20}{0.004} = 50\text{ s}$.

questionText: Based on Valence Bond Theory, what is the hybridization, geometry, and magnetic moment of $[FeF_6]^{3-}$?

options.text: $sp^3d^2$ hybridization; octahedral geometry; paramagnetic with $5$ unpaired electrons ($\mu \approx 5.92\text{ BM}$)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.text: $d^2sp^3$ hybridization; octahedral geometry; paramagnetic with $1$ unpaired electron
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: $sp^3d$ hybridization; trigonal bipyramidal geometry; diamagnetic
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: $dsp^2$ hybridization; square planar geometry; diamagnetic
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution: In $[FeF_6]^{3-}$, iron is in $+3$ state ($3d^5$). Fluoride ($F^-$) is a weak field ligand and cannot force electron pairing in the $3d$ subshell. The five $3d$ electrons remain unpaired ($n = 5$). The complex uses outer $4s, 4p,$ and $4d$ orbitals ($sp^3d^2$ hybridization, outer orbital octahedral), giving $\mu = \sqrt{5(7)} \approx 5.92\text{ BM}$.

questionText: Both $[Ni(CO)_4]$ and $[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$ are diamagnetic. What are their respective geometries and hybridizations according to VBT?

options.text: $[Ni(CO)_4]$ is tetrahedral ($sp^3$); $[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$ is square planar ($dsp^2$)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.text: $[Ni(CO)_4]$ is square planar ($dsp^2$); $[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$ is tetrahedral ($sp^3$)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: Both are tetrahedral ($sp^3$)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: Both are square planar ($dsp^2$)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution: In $[Ni(CO)_4]$, nickel is $Ni^0$ ($3d^8 4s^2$). Strong ligand $CO$ causes both $4s$ electrons to pair up into the $3d$ subshell, filling it completely ($3d^{10}$). The vacant $4s$ and three $4p$ orbitals undergo $sp^3$ hybridization, resulting in tetrahedral geometry (diamagnetic). In $[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$, nickel is $Ni^{2+}$ ($3d^8$). Strong ligand $CN^-$ pairs up the two unpaired $3d$ electrons, leaving one inner $3d$ orbital vacant. This vacant $3d$, one $4s$, and two $4p$ orbitals hybridize to form $dsp^2$ square planar geometry (diamagnetic).

One $4s$ and three $4p$ orbitals hybridize to form $sp^3$ tetrahedral complex. With 2 unpaired electrons ($n=2$), it is paramagnetic ($\mu \approx 2.84\text{ BM}$).

questionText: Why is the hexaamminecobalt(III) complex ion, $[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}$, diamagnetic and classified as an inner orbital complex?

options.text: The high $+3$ charge on cobalt causes sufficient crystal field splitting to pair all six 3d electrons into three orbitals, enabling $d^2sp^3$ hybridization
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.text: Cobalt is in a zero oxidation state with fully filled 4s subshell
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: Ammonia donates protons to reduce cobalt to $Co^+$
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: The complex adopts a regular tetrahedral geometry
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution: In $[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}$, cobalt is in the $+3$ oxidation state ($3d^6$). Despite ammonia being an intermediate ligand in the spectrochemical series, the high $+3$ nuclear charge of cobalt causes substantial orbital splitting, forcing all 6 electrons to pair up in three $3d$ orbitals. This leaves two inner $3d$ orbitals vacant, giving $d^2sp^3$ hybridization (diamagnetic, inner orbital octahedral complex).

questionText: Reaction of haloalkanes with potassium nitrite ($KNO_2$) predominantly yields alkyl nitrites ($R-ONO$), while reaction with silver nitrite ($AgNO_2$) predominantly yields nitroalkanes ($R-NO_2$). What explains this difference?

options.text: $KNO_2$ is ionic so attack occurs primarily through the electronegative oxygen atom bearing negative charge, whereas $AgNO_2$ is covalent so attack occurs through the nitrogen lone pair
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.text: $AgNO_2$ acts as an oxidizing agent that inserts oxygen into the $C-C$ bond
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: Potassium nitrite forms a sterically hindered cyclic intermediate that blocks nitrogen
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: Silver nitrite dissolves only in nonpolar solvents that prevent oxygen bonding
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution: Potassium nitrite is an ionic compound ($K^+ [O-N=O]^-$). The negative charge resides on oxygen, and the $C-O$ linkage forms easily, giving alkyl nitrite ($R-O-N=O$). In contrast, silver nitrite ($Ag-O-N=O$) is predominantly covalent; the nitrogen lone pair is more nucleophilic than the bonded oxygen, attacking the carbon to form a nitroalkane ($R-NO_2$).

questionText: When ethyl chloride is heated with a large excess of alcoholic ammonia in a sealed tube at $373\text{ K}$, what is the predominant amine product formed?

options.text: Ethylamine (primary amine)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.text: Diethylamine (secondary amine)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: Triethylamine (tertiary amine)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: Tetraethylammonium chloride (quaternary salt)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution: When an excess of ammonia is used, the probability of an alkyl halide molecule colliding with $NH_3$ is vastly greater than colliding with the newly formed primary amine. Thus, ethylamine ($CH_3CH_2NH_2$) is obtained as the predominant product. If alkyl halide were in excess, further alkylation would produce a mixture of $2^\circ, 3^\circ$ amines and quaternary ammonium salts.

questionText: When 2-bromobutane is heated with alcoholic potassium hydroxide ($KOH$), the predominant elimination product is:

options.text: But-2-ene (major product)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.text: But-1-ene (major product)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: But-1-yne
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: Butane
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution: According to Saytzeff's (Zaitsev's) rule, in dehydrohalogenation reactions, the preferred product is the alkene that has the greater number of alkyl groups attached to the doubly bonded carbon atoms (the more substituted and stable alkene). Elimination from 2-bromobutane can remove a proton from C1 or C3; removing from C3 gives the more substituted but-2-ene (~81% major product).

topic: Alcoholic KOH vs Aqueous KOH Role
questionText: Why does aqueous potassium hydroxide ($KOH$) promote substitution to give alcohols, whereas alcoholic potassium hydroxide ($KOH$) promotes $\beta$-elimination to give alkenes?

options.text: In alcohol, the ethoxide/alkoxide ion formed is a stronger base and less solvated than the heavily hydrated hydroxide ion in water
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.text: Aqueous $KOH$ is an acidic reagent that prevents proton abstraction
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: Alcoholic $KOH$ acts as an electrophilic reducing agent
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: Water converts the alkyl halide into a carboxylic acid before substitution
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution: In aqueous solution, hydroxide ions ($OH^-$) are heavily hydrated, which diminishes their basicity and favors nucleophilic substitution ($S_N$). In alcoholic solution (e.g., $KOH$ in ethanol), alkoxide ions ($C_2H_5O^-$) are formed. Alkoxide ions are much stronger bases and less solvated than hydrated hydroxide ions, favoring abstraction of a $\beta$-hydrogen and promoting elimination ($E2$) over substitution.

topic: Elimination Favored by Bulky Strong Bases
questionText: When 2-bromopropane is treated with potassium tert-butoxide ($KOC(CH_3)_3$), the predominant product formed is propene rather than tert-butyl isopropyl ether. Why?

options.text: The tert-butoxide ion is sterically bulky, hindering backside nucleophilic attack on carbon and favoring abstraction of an accessible $\beta$-proton
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.text: Potassium tert-butoxide is an extremely weak base that cannot displace bromide
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: The isopropyl group undergoes rapid free-radical halogenation instead of substitution
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: tert-Butoxide ion selectively cleaves the carbon-carbon single bond of the substrate
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution: Potassium tert-butoxide is a sterically hindered, bulky base. Its bulky methyl groups prevent it from easily approaching the electrophilic carbon to carry out an $S_N2$ displacement. Instead, it readily abstracts an exposed peripheral $\beta$-hydrogen, steering the reaction exclusively toward $E2$ $\beta$-elimination to form propene.

options.text: All three alcohols produce turbidity at identical rates at room temperature
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution: The Lucas test differentiates alcohols based on their reactivity with concentrated $HCl$ in the presence of anhydrous $ZnCl_2$. The reaction forms an insoluble alkyl chloride that appears as cloudiness (turbidity). Tertiary alcohols react instantaneously at room temperature. Secondary alcohols react within 5 minutes. Primary alcohols do not produce turbidity at room temperature, requiring heating.

topic: Mechanistic Basis of the Lucas Test
questionText: In the Lucas test, tertiary alcohols produce immediate cloudiness because the reaction proceeds via an $S_N1$ mechanism forming which stable intermediate?

options.text: A stable tertiary carbocation
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.text: A planar carbanion
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: A cyclic oxonium free radical
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: A pentacoordinate transition state without intermediates
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution: The reaction of alcohols with Lucas reagent proceeds via protonation and loss of water to form a carbocation intermediate ($S_N1$ mechanism). Because tertiary carbocations are highly stabilized by hyperconjugation and inductive effects, tertiary alcohols ionize immediately, leading to instantaneous formation of the insoluble tertiary alkyl chloride.

questionText: When ethanol is heated with excess concentrated sulfuric acid at $443\text{ K}$, ethene is formed, whereas heating excess ethanol with conc. $H_2SO_4$ at $413\text{ K}$ yields:

options.text: Diethyl ether (ethoxyethane) via bimolecular nucleophilic substitution ($S_N2$)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.text: Ethyl hydrogen sulfate crystals as the only stable end product
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: Ethanoic acid via oxidation
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: Acetylene gas with liberation of sulfur dioxide
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution: The dehydration of ethanol with conc. $H_2SO_4$ is highly temperature-dependent: At $443\text{ K}$ ($170^\circ\text{C}$), elimination ($E1$) dominates, yielding ethene: $C_2H_5OH \xrightarrow{H_2SO_4, 443\text{ K}} CH_2=CH_2 + H_2O$. At $413\text{ K}$ ($140^\circ\text{C}$) with excess ethanol, bimolecular nucleophilic substitution ($S_N2$) occurs between protonated ethanol and a second ethanol molecule, yielding diethyl ether: $2C_2H_5OH \xrightarrow{H_2SO_4, 413\text{ K}} C_2H_5OC_2H_5 + H_2O$.

questionText: What is the correct order of ease of dehydration among primary ($1^\circ$), secondary ($2^\circ$), and tertiary ($3^\circ$) alcohols in the presence of acid?

options.text: Tertiary ($3^\circ$) > Secondary ($2^\circ$) > Primary ($1^\circ$)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.text: Primary ($1^\circ$) > Secondary ($2^\circ$) > Tertiary ($3^\circ$)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: Secondary ($2^\circ$) > Tertiary ($3^\circ$) > Primary ($1^\circ$)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: Primary ($1^\circ$) > Tertiary ($3^\circ$) > Secondary ($2^\circ$)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution: Acid-catalyzed dehydration of alcohols involves protonation of the hydroxyl group followed by the loss of a water molecule to form a carbocation in the rate-determining step. The stability of carbocations follows the order $3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ$. Consequently, tertiary alcohols dehydrate under very mild conditions ($20\%\ H_3PO_4$ at $358\text{ K}$), secondary alcohols require $85\%\ H_3PO_4$ at $440\text{ K}$, and primary alcohols require conc. $H_2SO_4$ at $443\text{ K}$.

topic: Selective Oxidation of Primary Alcohols with PCC
questionText: Which reagent selectively oxidizes primary alcohols to aldehydes without causing over-oxidation to carboxylic acids?

options.text: Pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC) in anhydrous dichloromethane ($CH_2Cl_2$)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.text: Acidified potassium permanganate ($KMnO_4 / H_2SO_4$)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: Chromic acid ($H_2CrO_4$) in aqueous acetone
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: Nitric acid ($HNO_3$) under reflux
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution: Pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC, a complex of chromium trioxide with pyridine and $HCl$) in anhydrous dichloromethane is a mild and selective oxidizing agent. It oxidizes primary alcohols cleanly to aldehydes without oxidizing them further to carboxylic acids: $R-CH_2OH \xrightarrow{PCC, CH_2Cl_2} R-CHO$.

questionText: In the Wolff-Kishner reduction, a carbonyl compound is converted to an alkane. What sequence of reagents and reaction conditions is employed?

options.text: Reaction with hydrazine ($NH_2NH_2$) to form a hydrazone, followed by heating with $KOH$ in a high-boiling solvent like ethylene glycol
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.text: Reaction with hydroxylamine followed by treatment with phosphorus pentachloride
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: Treatment with sodium borohydride followed by concentrated sulfuric acid at $180^\circ\text{C}$
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: Hydrogenation over Raney nickel catalyst at room temperature and 1 atm pressure
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution: In the Wolff-Kishner reduction, aldehydes or ketones are heated with hydrazine ($NH_2NH_2$) to form a hydrazone intermediate. Subsequent heating with a strong base ($KOH$ or potassium tert-butoxide) in a high-boiling solvent such as ethylene glycol ($453-473\text{ K}$) causes evolution of nitrogen gas ($N_2$) and yields the alkane.

questionText: A chemist needs to reduce the carbonyl group of 4-chlorobutan-2-one ($CH_3COCH_2CH_2Cl$) to a methylene group. Why is Wolff-Kishner reduction NOT appropriate for this transformation?

options.text: The strong base ($KOH$) used at elevated temperatures will induce dehydrohalogenation or nucleophilic substitution of the alkyl chloride
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.text: Alkyl chlorides react violently with hydrazine to form explosive azides
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: Hydrazine cannot form a hydrazone when halogen atoms are present in the molecule
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: The basic conditions cause isomerization of the ketone to an aldehyde
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution: The Wolff-Kishner reduction utilizes strongly basic conditions ($KOH$ in hot glycol). Base-sensitive functional groups such as alkyl halides readily undergo dehydrohalogenation (elimination to alkene) or nucleophilic substitution by $OH^-$. In such cases, Clemmensen reduction or milder methods are used.

topic: Complex Metal Hydride Reductions (NaBH4 vs LiAlH4)
questionText: When an $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated ketone such as but-3-en-2-one ($CH_2=CH-COCH_3$) is treated with sodium borohydride ($NaBH_4$) in ethanol, what is the principal product obtained?

options.text: But-3-en-2-ol ($CH_2=CH-CH(OH)-CH_3$)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.text: Butan-2-one ($CH_3-CH_2-CO-CH_3$)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: Butan-2-ol ($CH_3-CH_2-CH(OH)-CH_3$)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: Butane ($CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-CH_3$)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution: Sodium borohydride ($NaBH_4$) is a selective reducing agent that reduces the carbonyl group of aldehydes and ketones to alcohols without affecting isolated or conjugated carbon-carbon double bonds under ordinary conditions. Thus, but-3-en-2-one is reduced cleanly to but-3-en-2-ol.

questionText: What is the composition of Tollens' reagent and what is observed when it is warmed with an aliphatic aldehyde?

options.text: Ammoniacal silver nitrate solution containing $[Ag(NH_3)_2]^+$; a bright silver mirror forms on the inner wall of the test tube
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.text: Aqueous copper sulfate and sodium hydroxide; a bright red precipitate of $Cu_2O$ is produced
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: Solution of potassium iodide and iodine; a yellow precipitate of $CHI_3$ separates
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: Neutral ferric chloride solution; a deep violet-purple complex is produced
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution: Tollens' reagent is freshly prepared ammoniacal silver nitrate, $[Ag(NH_3)_2]^+OH^-$. On warming with an aldehyde, the aldehyde is oxidized to a carboxylate anion while the silver(I) complex ion is reduced to metallic silver: $RCHO + 2[Ag(NH_3)_2]^+ + 3OH^- \to RCOO^- + 2Ag\downarrow + 2H_2O + 4NH_3$. The metallic silver deposits as a shiny mirror.

questionText: Does benzaldehyde give a positive Tollens' test, and what is the chemical equation representing this behavior?

options.text: Yes, benzaldehyde reduces Tollens' reagent to metallic silver while being oxidized to benzoate ion
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.text: No, aromatic aldehydes are resistant to all mild oxidizing agents including Tollens' reagent
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: No, benzaldehyde undergoes Cannizzaro reaction with ammonia instead of reducing silver ions
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: Yes, benzaldehyde gives a red precipitate of cuprous oxide with Tollens' reagent
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution: Both aliphatic and aromatic aldehydes reduce Tollens' reagent. Benzaldehyde is oxidized to the benzoate anion ($C_6H_5COO^-$) while silver ions ($Ag^+$) are reduced to elemental silver ($Ag$), producing a silver mirror. Tollens' test distinguishes aldehydes (both aliphatic and aromatic) from ketones.

topic: Reaction of Tertiary Aliphatic Amines with Nitrous Acid
questionText: How do tertiary aliphatic amines such as triethylamine react with cold nitrous acid?

options.text: They dissolve to form clear, water-soluble trialkylammonium nitrite salts ($[R_3NH]^+NO_2^-$) without evolution of gas
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.text: They evolve nitrogen gas and form tertiary alcohols
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: They undergo oxidative cleavage into secondary amines and formaldehyde
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: They form a bright red insoluble nitroso derivative
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution: Tertiary aliphatic amines lack replaceable hydrogen atoms on nitrogen. When treated with cold nitrous acid, they merely undergo acid-base neutralization to form water-soluble trialkylammonium nitrite salts: $R_3N + HNO_2 \rightleftharpoons [R_3NH]^+NO_2^-$. No nitrogen gas is evolved.

questionText: What chemical compound is known as the Hinsberg reagent and used to distinguish between primary, secondary, and tertiary amines?

options.text: Benzenesulphonyl chloride ($C_6H_5SO_2Cl$)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.text: Benzoyl chloride ($C_6H_5COCl$)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: p-Toluenesulfonic acid ($p-CH_3C_6H_4SO_3H$)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: Benzenesulfonic acid ($C_6H_5SO_3H$)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution: The Hinsberg reagent is benzenesulphonyl chloride ($C_6H_5SO_2Cl$). It reacts differently with primary, secondary, and tertiary amines depending on the number of replaceable hydrogen atoms bonded to the nitrogen atom.

questionText: When ethanamine is shaken with benzenesulphonyl chloride in aqueous $KOH$, the resulting sulphonamide dissolves completely in the alkaline solution. Why is it soluble in alkali?

options.text: The sulphonamide (N-ethylbenzenesulphonamide) contains an acidic hydrogen on nitrogen attached to the strongly electron-withdrawing $-SO_2-$ group, forming a water-soluble potassium salt
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.text: The sulphonamide decomposes into water-soluble potassium sulfate and ethylamine
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: The product is non-polar and dissolves in water via hydrophobic interactions
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: The lone pair on sulfur forms a covalent coordinate bond with potassium ion
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution: The reaction of a primary amine with benzenesulphonyl chloride yields an N-alkylbenzenesulphonamide: $C_6H_5SO_2Cl + RNH_2 \to C_6H_5SO_2NHR + HCl$. The hydrogen atom attached to nitrogen is strongly acidic due to the powerful electron-withdrawing effect of the adjacent sulfonyl ($-SO_2-$) group. Consequently, it dissolves in aqueous alkali ($KOH$ or $NaOH$) to form a water-soluble salt: $C_6H_5SO_2N^-(K^+)R$.

questionText: When diethylamine reacts with benzenesulphonyl chloride, the product formed remains insoluble in aqueous potassium hydroxide ($KOH$). What is the reason for its insolubility?

options.text: The product (N,N-diethylbenzenesulphonamide) has no acidic hydrogen atom attached to the nitrogen atom and cannot form an alkali salt
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.text: The product undergoes instant polymerization into an insoluble resin
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: Potassium hydroxide hydrolyzes the product back into insoluble diethyl ether
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: The sulfonyl group becomes positively charged in basic solution, repelling hydroxide ions
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution: Secondary amines react with benzenesulphonyl chloride to form N,N-dialkylbenzenesulphonamides: $C_6H_5SO_2Cl + R_2NH \to C_6H_5SO_2NR_2 + HCl$. Because there is no hydrogen atom attached to the nitrogen in this product, it lacks acidic character and is completely insoluble in aqueous alkali, separating as an insoluble solid or oil.

questionText: What happens when a tertiary amine such as triethylamine is treated with the Hinsberg reagent ($C_6H_5SO_2Cl$) in the presence of aqueous alkali?

options.text: No reaction occurs because tertiary amines lack any hydrogen atom directly attached to nitrogen
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.text: It forms a soluble quaternary sulphonamide salt
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: It decomposes with vigorous evolution of sulfur dioxide gas
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: It oxidizes immediately into a bright green nitro compound
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution: Tertiary amines do not have any hydrogen atom bonded to the nitrogen atom and therefore do not react with benzenesulphonyl chloride under Hinsberg test conditions. The unreacted tertiary amine remains insoluble in aqueous alkali but dissolves when the mixture is acidified with mineral acid.

questionText: Which naturally occurring $\alpha$-amino acid is optically INACTIVE (achiral)?

options.text: Glycine
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.text: L-Alanine
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: L-Valine
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: L-Serine
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution: In glycine, the side chain $\text{R}$ is a single hydrogen atom ($\text{H}_2\text{N}-\text{CH}_2-\text{COOH}$). Because the $\alpha$-carbon is bonded to two identical hydrogen atoms, it lacks four different substituent groups and is therefore achiral (optically inactive). All other 19 common $\alpha-amino acids contain an asymmetric $\alpha-carbon and are optically active.

topic: Configuration of Naturally Occurring Amino Acids
questionText: Most naturally occurring $\alpha$-amino acids obtained from proteins have which stereochemical configuration at the $\alpha$-carbon?

options.text: L-configuration (with the $-NH_2$ group positioned on the left in the Fischer projection)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: Meso configuration due to internal symmetry planes
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution: All naturally occurring optically active $\alpha$-amino acids found in proteins belong to the L-series. When drawn in a standard Fischer projection with the $-COOH$ group at the top and the $\text{R}$ group at the bottom, the $-NH_2$ group is on the left-hand side, representing the L-configuration.

questionText: In neutral aqueous solution, $\alpha$-amino acids exist predominantly as internal dipolar salts known as zwitterions. What is the ionic structure of this zwitterion?

options.text: $\text{H}_3\text{N}^+-\text{CH}(\text{R})-\text{COO}^-$
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.text: $\text{H}_2\text{N}-\text{CH}(\text{R})-\text{COOH}$
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: $\text{H}_3\text{N}^+-\text{CH}(\text{R})-\text{COOH}$
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: $\text{H}_2\text{N}-\text{CH}(\text{R})-\text{COO}^-$
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution: In aqueous solution, an intramolecular proton transfer occurs where the acidic carboxyl group ($-COOH$) loses a proton to form a carboxylate anion ($-COO^-$), while the basic amino group ($-NH_2$) accepts that proton to form an ammonium cation ($-NH_3^+$). This dipolar ion with both positive and negative charges is called a zwitterion: $\text{H}_3\text{N}^+-\text{CH}(\text{R})-\text{COO}^-$.

questionText: Why do $\alpha$-amino acid zwitterions display amphoteric behavior in aqueous solution?

options.text: The $-COO^-$ group can accept a proton from acids, while the $-NH_3^+$ group can donate a proton to bases
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.text: The $\alpha$-carbon undergoes reversible homolytic cleavage in aqueous acid or base
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: The hydrocarbon side chain ($\text{R}$) reacts equally with both hydronium and hydroxide ions
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: The zwitterion acts exclusively as an oxidizing agent in water
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution: In the zwitterionic form, the basic carboxylate ion ($-COO^-$) can accept a proton in acidic solution to form a cation ($\text{H}_3\text{N}^+-\text{CH}(\text{R})\text{COOH}$), and the acidic ammonium ion ($-NH_3^+$) can donate a proton in basic solution to form an anion ($\text{H}_2\text{N}-\text{CH}(\text{R})\text{COO}^-$). Because they react with both acids and bases, amino acids are amphoteric.

questionText: What is the isoelectric point (pI) of an amino acid, and how does the amino acid behave in an electric field at this specific pH?

options.text: The pH at which the net electrical charge on the amino acid is zero; it does not migrate toward either electrode during electrophoresis
options.mistakeAnalysis: Follows standard NCERT derivation and principle

options.text: The pH at which all peptide bonds in the amino acid are spontaneously hydrolysed
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: The pH at which the amino acid carries a net $+2$ charge and migrates rapidly to the cathode
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

options.text: The pH at which the amino acid reaches its minimum boiling point in solution
options.mistakeAnalysis: Student miscalculated or applied wrong principle

detailedSolution: The isoelectric point (pI) is the characteristic pH at which the dipolar zwitterion concentration is maximal and the net electrical charge of the amino acid is exactly zero. At its isoelectric point, an amino acid does not migrate toward either the cathode or the anode when placed in an electric field.
